title: 200 Indian Americans Walked Into 125 Congressional Offices in One Day. Here's What They Asked For.
excerpt: The fourth annual FIIDS Capitol Hill Day tripled its inaugural turnout, pressing lawmakers on green card reform, critical minerals, and the US-India defence corridor.
body:
The Indian American community just staged its largest-ever legislative push on Capitol Hill — and the agenda reads like a playbook for Washington's own strategic anxieties.

On 23 June, nearly 200 delegates from 25 states fanned out across more than 125 Congressional offices in Washington, D.C., in the fourth annual Capitol Hill Day organised by the Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies (FIIDS). The turnout nearly tripled the 70 delegates who showed up when the initiative launched in 2023, and represented the biggest coordinated lobby effort by Indian Americans to date.

## Five Priorities, One Message

The delegates carried a tightly focused five-point platform: deepening Indo-Pacific trade and security, strengthening the US-India strategic partnership, reforming high-skilled immigration programmes, recognising Indian American contributions, and securing critical minerals supply chains.

That last item is new this year — and tells its own story. Critical minerals have become a bipartisan obsession in Washington as lawmakers scramble to reduce dependence on China-dominated supply chains for everything from semiconductors to electric vehicle batteries. India, with its own reserves of rare earth elements, lithium, and cobalt, and its growing refining ambitions, sits at the intersection of that anxiety. FIIDS delegates framed it explicitly: India is not just a trade partner — it is a supply-chain alternative to China, and Congress needs to act on that before the window closes.

'This is a moment to translate influence into policy impact,' said Khanderao Kand, FIIDS Chief of Policy and Strategy. 'Our community is engaged in ensuring that Congress understands the issues that matter most to America's future.'

## The Green Card Backlog That Won't Go Away

Immigration reform remains the most personal item on the agenda. The delegates pressed lawmakers on the seven per cent per-country cap on employment-based green cards — a provision that has created a backlog stretching decades for Indian nationals. An estimated 400,000 Indian-born applicants are currently waiting, with some facing projected wait times of 80 years or more under current rules.

For the thousands of H-1B professionals who have built careers, bought homes, and raised American-born children while stuck in this queue, the issue is existential. Several bills addressing the backlog have been introduced in Congress over the years — including the Eagle Act and the Fairness for High-Skilled Immigrants Act — but none has cleared both chambers. FIIDS delegates were direct with lawmakers: the per-country cap punishes demand, not merit, and it sends talent to Canada, Australia, and the UK while America waits.

The issue cuts across party lines. Republican offices heard the argument framed as economic competitiveness — America risks losing its edge if it forces skilled immigrants to wait decades. Democratic offices heard it framed as fairness — a cap that disadvantages one nationality amounts to structural discrimination. FIIDS tailored the pitch to the room.

## A Partnership Summit to Match

The advocacy sessions were followed by the US-India Partnership Summit, where Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Bethany Morrison and Deputy Chief of Mission Ambassador Mangya Khampa headlined alongside other senior diplomats. The summit reviewed bilateral cooperation across defence, technology, clean energy, and the Quad — an agenda that mirrors the priorities the delegates had just carried into Congressional offices hours earlier.

Morrison's presence was notable. As Deputy Assistant Secretary in the Bureau of South and Central Asian Affairs, she oversees the day-to-day management of the US-India relationship. Her willingness to headline a diaspora-organised event signals that the State Department views Indian American advocacy not as a peripheral constituency exercise but as a strategic channel.

## Why It Matters for the Diaspora

The Indian American community now numbers over four million, with outsized influence in technology, healthcare, academia, and entrepreneurship. But political representation has lagged behind economic clout. There are currently five Indian-American members of the House of Representatives — the largest cohort ever — but no Indian American has served in the Senate.

Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, who has championed green card reform legislation, has been blunt about the stakes. 'If you don't have a seat at the table, you're on the menu,' he told FIIDS delegates at a previous Capitol Hill Day. 'It's time to run for office. I don't care if you're a Republican, independent, or Democrat.'

The growth trajectory suggests the message is landing. From 70 delegates in 2023 to 132 in 2024 to 145 in 2025 and now nearly 200, the annual push is becoming a fixture on the Congressional calendar — and a signal that the Indian American community is learning to play the Washington game on its own terms.
